newsitem.title: UK: British voters ignored anti-European rhetoric.
newsitem.headline: British voters ignored anti-European rhetoric.

text.p: The future of Britain's relations with the European Union dominated the Conservative government's election campaign but the finer points of their argument were trampled in a landslide swing to Labour.

The outgoing Conservatives were left on Friday to ponder the abject failure of their attempts to convince voters that Labour would sell out Britain to EU partners set on building "a federalist superstate".

When John Major won the last general election in 1992 with a majority of 21, he vowed Britain would be at the centre of Europe but his Conservatives hardened their line in a bid to divert attention away from the deep splits within their own ranks over relations with the EU.

At the height of the six-week election campaign for Thursday's vote, the Conservatives ran newspaper advertisements portraying Labour leader Tony Blair as a ventriloquist's dummy perched on the knee of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
The voters took no notice at all, preferring to mow down scores of Conservative legislators including, some of the most committed "Eurosceptics" opposed to closer ties with the EU.
Perhaps the greatest scalp was that of Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, who made a ferociously anti-EU speech at the Conservative party conference in 1995.
"Going Eurosceptic did not help us one jot," said pro-EU legislator Edwina Currie, a former junion agriculture minister who also lost her seat.
To the Eurosceptics' dismay, both Major and his finance minister, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, refused to rule out taking Britain into European Monetary Union (EMU).

More than 200 Conservative candidates in an election in which 659 seats were contested openly defied Major by issuing campaign leaflets saying they opposed Britain ever signing up to a planned EU single currency, an act of rebellion which only highlighted the party's divisions.
The recriminations flowed quickly -- Eurosceptic Conservative MP Nicholas Winterton said Clarke would be "reviled in history" for his refusal to rule out a single European currency.

The waters were considerably muddied by billionaire anti-European entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith, who spent millions of pounds of his own money setting up the Referendum Party to press for a referendum on ties with the EU.

The Conservatives, worried that he might siphon off crucial votes in marginal constituencies, also promised a referendum. But in the end it did them no good, even though Goldsmith's candidates were routed.
Tom Spencer, the head of the Conservatives in the European parliament, said party leaders had lost their heads.

"The party's obsession with the possibility that tens of thousands of people might vote for the Referendum Party was shown...to be a complete irrelevance in comparison to the missing millions of Tory voters who voted Liberal Democrat, Labour or just stayed home in disgust," he said.
Spencer also attacked prominent Eurosceptic right-winger John Redwood, who unsuccessfully challenged Major for the party leadership in 1995 and took a hard line on EMU.

"I cannot this morning suppress my contempt for John Redwood's action in setting up a party within a party' and deliberately igniting the single currency issue at a crucial moment in the campaign," Spencer said in a statement.
